fields.definition: The pulsing tremolo effect produced by a vibraphone's motor-driven rotating discs (fans) fitted at the tops of its resonator tubes; as the discs spin they alternately open and close the resonators, cyclically varying the amplitude of each sustaining note. Motor speed sets the rate (roughly 1-12 Hz), and the motor can be switched off for a plain, steady tone.
fields.plain_english: It is the wavering, pulsing sound of a vibraphone. A small motor spins discs inside the tubes under the bars. They open and close, so each note gets louder and softer over and over, like a slow shimmer.
fields.purpose_function: It gives the vibraphone its signature shimmering sustain, adding motion to held notes, and the variable-speed motor lets a player match the vibrato rate to the music or switch it off entirely.
fields.practical_application: A player sets the motor speed to taste while an engineer mikes the instrument; because the effect is acoustic amplitude modulation it must be captured at the source rather than added convincingly afterward.
common_mistakes: Calling the effect true vibrato when it is actually tremolo (amplitude modulation), not a change in pitch.
Assuming the spinning discs change the pitch of the bars; they only vary how strongly the resonators reinforce each note.
Setting the motor very fast and expecting a classic sound, when most classic parts use a slow rate or no motor at all.
scenario_contexts: Recording a jazz vibraphone solo and choosing a slow motor speed for a warm, shimmering sustain.
Performing a classical mallet part with the motor switched off for a clean, steady tone.
Miking a vibraphone in a live band and blending both sides of the bars to capture the vibrato evenly.

sources: Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (2nd ed.), mallet/idiophone chapter
Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians, 'Vibraphone'
Adler, The Study of Orchestration, percussion chapter

fields.definition: The rattling, buzzing sustain of a vibraslap, a percussion instrument descended from the quijada (donkey jawbone). Striking the wooden ball on its bent metal rod jars a set of loose pins or rivets held in a hollow resonating box, which vibrate against the box to produce a sharp crack followed by a long, dry buzz.
fields.plain_english: It is the loud, rattling sound a vibraslap makes. You hit the wooden ball, and loose metal pins inside a wooden box shake and buzz. It is like a fast wooden rattle that slowly fades.
fields.purpose_function: The buzz delivers a sudden accent with a long, decaying rattle, used to punctuate hits and transitions where a plain, short strike would not carry enough character.
fields.practical_application: A percussionist holds the metal rod loosely and slaps the ball with the palm, then lifts or damps the instrument to control how long the buzz rings; engineers pad the channel because the initial crack is very loud.
common_mistakes: Gripping the metal rod tightly, which chokes the buzz and shortens the sustain.
Striking the wooden box instead of the ball, which produces a weak, uneven rattle.
Forgetting that the initial crack is very loud, then clipping the channel or startling nearby microphones.
scenario_contexts: Adding a rattling accent at the end of a phrase in a Latin or pop percussion arrangement.
Using the vibraslap for a comedic or dramatic shudder effect in film or theatre sound.
Layering a short buzzing hit into a drum track to mark a transition or fill.

sources: Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians, 'Vibraslap' / 'Quijada'
Blades, Percussion Instruments and Their History
Adler, The Study of Orchestration, percussion chapter

fields.definition: The sharp, dry transient that begins a wood block's sound. A wood block is a hollow, slotted hardwood block; struck with a stick or hard mallet it produces a bright, high click with a very fast onset and short decay, giving it one of the crispest attacks in the percussion section.
fields.plain_english: It is the quick, hard knock you hear the instant a wood block is hit. The sound starts almost at once and dies away fast. Think of the sharp click of a clock tick, but louder and more woody.
fields.purpose_function: The fast, clear attack lets a wood block cut through a mix and mark rhythm precisely, which is why it is used for clave patterns, sound effects, and tight rhythmic accents.
fields.practical_application: Because the attack is so fast and loud, an engineer uses a microphone that tracks quick transients and may trim the fader or add light compression so the click sits in the mix without spiking the meters.
common_mistakes: Confusing the wood block's attack with its pitch; the sharp onset is a timing and transient feature, not the note's fundamental.
Over-compressing the channel, which softens the very transient that makes the wood block useful.
Miking too far away, so the crisp attack is lost and only a dull thud remains.
scenario_contexts: Recording a clave or wood block part where the crisp attack must line up tightly with the beat.
Reinforcing a percussion section live and keeping the wood block's click audible over a loud band.
Using a wood block hit as a sharp sound effect, such as a knock or clock tick, in post production.

sources: Adler, The Study of Orchestration, percussion chapter
Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians, 'Wood block'
Ballou (ed.), Handbook for Sound Engineers, on transient/envelope (attack)

fields.definition: The bright, sharp onset of a xylophone note. The xylophone's hard rosewood or synthetic bars, struck with hard mallets, produce a fast, percussive attack and short sustain; the bars are quint-tuned (the strong overtone a twelfth above the fundamental), reinforcing the brilliant, brittle character of the attack.
fields.plain_english: It is the bright, hard ping at the start of each xylophone note. The wooden bars are hit with hard mallets, so the sound jumps out fast and fades quickly. It sounds sharper and drier than a marimba.
fields.purpose_function: The strong attack makes the xylophone cut clearly through an ensemble and articulate fast passages, which is why it is chosen for crisp, bright melodic lines and rhythmic figures.
fields.practical_application: An engineer mikes the xylophone to capture the bright transient without harshness, often adding distance or a slight high-frequency roll-off to tame the sharp attack in a dense mix.
common_mistakes: Confusing the xylophone with the marimba; the xylophone has a brighter, drier, sharper attack and a higher range.
Using soft mallets and expecting the characteristic sharp attack, when hard mallets are what create it.
Boosting high frequencies to add brightness, which can make the already sharp attack harsh and brittle.
scenario_contexts: Recording a fast xylophone melody where each note's sharp attack must stay clean and distinct.
Mixing a xylophone into an orchestral track and controlling its bright transient so it cuts without piercing.
Reinforcing xylophone in live musical theatre so its articulation is heard over the pit.

sources: Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (2nd ed.), bar-percussion tuning
Adler, The Study of Orchestration, percussion chapter
Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians, 'Xylophone'
